question: Q1  Are train and test distributed alike?
what the evidence shows: Promotions follow one chain-wide calendar (stores disagree on 0 of 900 dates), Monday to Friday only, in alternating weeks. Promotion share is similar in the same season (39.6% in test and in 2014). School holidays are 44% of test days vs 23% across train, but 43% in the same season of 2014.
what it means for the business: The test window is a summer window: promotion rhythm is familiar, school-holiday exposure is much higher than in most of the training period.
what the data cannot establish: Whether the 2015 summer behaves like earlier summers (only 2013 and part of 2014 exist).

question: Q2  Sales before, during and after holidays
what the evidence shows: Stores are almost all closed on state holidays (about 2% open). Open stores sell about 40% more than a normal day in the 3 days before Easter and 19% more before Christmas; the 3 days after Easter sell 12% less. School holidays show no consistent change on ordinary days.
what it means for the business: Holiday weeks need their own features: a run-up uplift before, a closure on the day, and a lull after Easter.
what the data cannot establish: Holiday effects rest on only 3 Easters, 2 Christmases and 14 national holidays; regional holidays were excluded.

question: Q3  Seasonal (Christmas, Easter) behaviour
what the evidence shows: December is the peak (about 1.22 times a normal day in both years). The 15 to 23 December run-up averages 1.49, but 24 December falls to 0.71. January is the low point (0.94). Spring 2015 runs above spring 2013 and 2014.
what it means for the business: Sales are strongly seasonal and the pattern repeats year to year, so calendar features should carry most of it.
what the data cannot establish: Only two full years: a different 2015 pattern cannot be ruled out.

question: Q4  Sales and customers
what the evidence shows: Correlation 0.83 across all open days (customers explain 68% of the variation) and 0.95 inside a typical store. Spend per customer ranges from 5.1 (type b) to 11.2 (type d).
what it means for the business: Customers are the main driver of sales, but customers are not available in the test period, so the model must predict sales without them.
what the data cannot establish: Correlation does not show that more customers cause more sales, and customers cannot be split into new and returning.

question: Q5  How promotions affect sales and customers
what the evidence shows: On ordinary Monday-to-Friday days, promotions raise sales by 39%, customers by 20% and spend per customer by 16%. Every store gains (median 39%, range 2% to 103%). Saturdays after promotion weeks are 3% busier, not quieter.
what it means for the business: Promotions bring both more shoppers and bigger baskets, with no sign of a hangover in the following days.
what the data cannot establish: Not causal (promotions were not randomised), and the data cannot separate existing customers from new ones.

question: Q6  Where promotions could be deployed more effectively
what the evidence shows: Every store follows the same calendar, so differences come from response. Lift is lowest for type b (15%) and assortment b (12%) stores; larger stores gain less in percent (34% vs 43%) but more in money (2,845 vs 1,576 extra sales a promotion day). Lift is strongest on Mondays (+57%) and weakest on Fridays (+22%).
what it means for the business: If promotions cost money or can be targeted, the weakest responders (type b, assortment b) are the first to review; the strongest are small and mid-sized stores.
what the data cannot establish: Without promotion costs or margins, profitability cannot be judged; no store ever ran a different promotion calendar to compare.

question: Q7  Customer behaviour around opening and closing
what the evidence shows: Customers peak on Monday (858) and are lowest on Saturday (662). After a closure of a week or more, sales on the reopening day are 2.6 times typical; before such a closure they run at 0.59.
what it means for the business: Closures matter for forecasting: sales dip before a long closure and rebound afterwards, so days since reopening is a useful feature.
what the data cannot establish: The data is daily: opening and closing hours and customer flow within a day cannot be studied.

question: Q8  Stores open on all weekdays and their weekend sales
what the evidence shows: 1,109 of 1,115 stores are open on at least 95% of ordinary Monday-to-Friday days. Only 33 stores trade on Sundays (all 17 type b stores and all 9 assortment-b stores). Among type a stores, Sunday traders keep their Saturday sales (Saturday = 0.82 of a weekday vs 0.74) and their Monday-to-Saturday total is within 2% of similar stores that close on Sundays, so Sunday sales look largely additional.
what it means for the business: Sunday trading does not appear to take sales from Saturday, but it is rare and tied to store type.
what the data cannot establish: Only 13 comparable stores; Sunday trading is not randomly assigned, so it cannot be called the cause.

question: Q9  Assortment type and sales
what the evidence shows: Average store sales per day: a 6,602, b 8,503, c 7,287. Like with like, extended assortment sells more in type a (+18%) and type d (+9%), but less in type c (-7%).
what it means for the business: Assortment alone does not explain sales: store type matters more, and the effect of a bigger range depends on the store type.
what the data cannot establish: All 9 assortment-b stores are type b, so 'extra' assortment cannot be separated from store type.

question: Q10  Competitor distance
what the evidence shows: Little relationship: rank correlation -0.03 overall (type a -0.09, c -0.01, d 0.06). Stores with a competitor under 500 m have more customers (870 vs 582) but smaller baskets (7.8 vs 11.0).
what it means for the business: Distance to a competitor is a weak predictor of store sales on its own; it is more useful together with the date a competitor opened.
what the data cannot establish: There is no location information, so the city-centre question cannot be tested; short distances are only a hint of dense areas.

question: Q11  Competitor opening and reopening
what the evidence shows: For 120 stores with a competitor opening in the data, sales fall 7.1% on average in the 3 months after opening (chance range -0.9% to 1.2%); 80% of stores fell. The fall is 14% for competitors under 1 km, 9% for 1 to 5 km and about zero beyond 5 km.
what it means for the business: A new nearby competitor costs a store roughly a tenth of its sales, partly recovered by month 3; competitor opening date and distance are valuable features.
what the data cannot establish: store.csv is a single snapshot, so a distance that changes from missing to known cannot be seen; 356 stores have no usable opening date; opening dates are only accurate to the month.
